props.title: What is an acoustic band, and is it quieter than an electric one?
props.seo_title: What is an acoustic band, and is it quieter than an electric one?
props.dek: "Acoustic" describes the instruments, and some acoustic instruments are loud. Here's what the word means to a musician, why a drum kit is louder than an electric guitar, and how to choose for your venue's volume limit.
props.meta_description: Acoustic or electric band for your event? What each one means, which is actually quieter, upright vs electric bass, and how Colorado volume limits change the choice.
props.llms_description: What is an acoustic band, and is acoustic quieter than electric? Written by Signet Artists' founder, a working bass player in Denver. Acoustic instruments make their own sound, and most acoustic acts still use a small sound system for the voice. An acoustic drum kit or trumpet is loud and can only be played so softly, while an electric guitar can be turned down to almost any level, so the useful question for a quiet event is which instruments are in the band. The post compares upright and electric bass, gives Colorado's state outdoor noise limit for residential zones (55 dB(A) by day, 50 dB(A) at night), and suggests an act for a dinner, a cocktail hour followed by dancing, a weekly night at a bar or lobby, and a venue with a strict limit.

hero.alt: Two acoustic guitars and an electric guitar on stands by a sunlit window, with a keyboard beside them.

items.text: Acoustic instruments make their own sound. Most acoustic acts still use a small sound system for the voice.
An electric instrument can be turned down to almost any level. A drum kit can only go so low.
Give the band your venue's volume limit, and let them choose the instruments to fit it.

props.html: When a planner asks for something acoustic, they usually mean music their guests can talk over. That’s a fair thing to want. The word gets you partway there.

To a musician, an acoustic instrument makes sound on its own: a guitar, an upright bass, a piano, a violin, a trumpet, a drum kit. An electric instrument needs an amplifier: an electric guitar, an electric bass, a keyboard.

Most acoustic acts still plug something in. A singer needs a microphone to be heard past the first few tables, and a guitar often has a pickup so it can reach the back of a ballroom. An acoustic duo usually means two acoustic instruments and a small sound system, set low.

A drum kit and a trumpet are both acoustic, and both are loud. A drummer can play softly, with brushes or thin rods in place of sticks, but there’s a floor below which a drum kit stops sounding like one.

An electric guitar through a small amplifier has no floor. The volume is a knob, and the guitarist can sit it at almost any level the venue asks for.

So for a quiet event, the useful question is which instruments are in the band, and whether one of them is a drum kit.

I play both for a living, and they do different jobs.

An upright bass is warm and soft at the front of each note, and it looks the part for jazz and a cocktail hour. In a big space or outdoors, it needs a pickup and an amplifier to be heard. An electric bass is tighter and more even from note to note, and it’s easier to keep at one steady level. It’s the usual choice for funk, pop and a dance floor.

Most venues have a number, even when nobody mentions it until the week of the event.

Outdoors, Colorado’s state limit in a residential zone is 55 dB(A) from 7am to 7pm and 50 dB(A) after that, measured 25 feet or more beyond the property line. We go through what that means in what changes when the reception is outdoors. Denver has its own noise ordinance too, in Chapter 36 of the city code. Hotels and restaurants often set their own level for a ballroom or a patio.

Whatever the number is, give it to the band when you book. That number decides more about the instruments than the word acoustic does. Here’s how loud background music should be, and the levels for each size of band are on our technical page.

• Guests talk the whole time (a client dinner, a reception): a solo player or an acoustic duo, no drums.
  • A cocktail hour, then dancing: one band that starts small and acoustic and adds drums and electric instruments later. Here’s how one band covers a whole wedding day.
  • Music every week at a bar or a lobby: a solo act with a small system, at the level of a conversation at the next table. That’s our weekly live music program.
  • A strict limit or neighbors close by: fewer drums, more strings.
